planting.note: Separate rosette offsets from established clumps in spring and pot in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; cathedral window haworthia grows naturally tucked among rocks in dappled shade in South Africa's Eastern Cape, so it wants bright indirect light rather than direct sun, making it one of the easier soft-leaved succulents for an east- or north-facing windowsill.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a shallow pot of gritty, fast-draining cactus mix, and let the soil dry out between waterings. Haworthia cymbiformis forms a low, dense rosette of plump, pale-green, boat-shaped leaves whose translucent, rounded tips act as tiny windows, letting light reach photosynthetic tissue deeper in the leaf when the plant is naturally half-buried in sandy soil in the wild. It offsets readily around the base, quickly forming a tight cluster of rosettes that can be divided every couple of years to make new plants. Unlike hard-leaved zebra-type haworthias, its leaves are soft, glossy, and nearly translucent along the margins, and the whole rosette plumps or wrinkles noticeably to signal watering needs. It tolerates lower light than almost any other succulent, making it a reliable choice for a bright bathroom or office desk as well as a classic windowsill spot, and it sends up thin, wiry stems of small white summer flowers that are easily trimmed off if not wanted.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; panda plant rarely flowers or sets viable seed in home cultivation, so it is propagated almost exclusively from cuttings and offsets rather than seed.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct morning sun in very well-drained, gritty cactus mix, watering only after the soil has dried completely. Kalanchoe tomentosa (panda plant) is a Madagascar native prized for its thick, silvery-grey, felted leaves edged in chocolate-brown scalloped markings that resemble a panda's ears, with a dense coat of fine hairs covering the whole plant. Water at the soil line rather than overhead, since the fuzzy leaves trap moisture against the surface and are prone to rot or unsightly spotting if wetted; the same fuzz makes leaf-cutting propagation less reliable than stem cuttings, which root readily in a few weeks. Left to its own devices it forms an upright, sparsely branched shrublet on a windowsill or in a container, and leggy stems can be pinched or cut back hard to encourage bushier new growth from the base.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Press or lightly bury the small plantlets that drop from mature leaf margins onto moist, well-drained succulent mix in spring or summer; each plantlet already has tiny roots forming and establishes within days, so propagation is essentially automatic once a plant is producing them.

directions: Grow in bright light, including some direct sun, in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only when the soil has dried out. Kalanchoe daigremontiana (mother of thousands, alligator plant) forms an upright rosette of long, grey-green, purple-blotched leaves edged with rows of miniature plantlets that root wherever they touch soil, a reproductive strategy that gives the plant its common name and makes it one of the most effortlessly propagated houseplants in cultivation. Because of that same trait it self-sows aggressively and is classified as invasive in frost-free parts of the Gulf Coast, Florida, Hawaii, and other subtropical regions, so it is best confined to a container on a windowsill or patio rather than planted in the ground in warm climates, and spent flower stalks or dropped plantlets should be cleaned up promptly. All parts contain cardiac glycosides (bufadienolides) that are toxic if ingested by pets or livestock, so site it out of reach of curious animals and children.

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; silver dollar jade is slow-growing and eventually forms a small, gnarled, tree-like trunk, so container culture with occasional repotting into a slightly larger pot suits it well.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry between waterings. Crassula arborescens (silver dollar jade, silver jade plant) is a South African relative of the common jade plant, distinguished by larger, nearly circular, powdery blue-grey leaves edged in red that intensifies with bright light and cooler temperatures. It grows more slowly and stays more compact for longer than Crassula ovata, but over years develops a similar thick, woody, tree-like trunk and can be trained as a striking succulent bonsai in a shallow container. Propagate from stem or leaf cuttings allowed to callus for a day or two before rooting in dry succulent mix; established plants tolerate brief dry spells well but are quick to rot if left in soggy soil, especially in winter. Small pale-pink, star-shaped flower clusters may appear in late winter on mature specimens grown in strong light.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; the fine hairs covering the leaves make leaf-propagation less reliable than in smooth-leaved echeverias, so stem cuttings are the preferred home method.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering only after the soil has dried out completely. Echeveria pulvinata (plush plant) is a Mexican succulent covered from stem to leaf tip in a soft coat of fine white hairs that gives the whole rosette a velvety, chenille-like texture unlike smooth-leaved echeverias. The leaf tips and margins flush a vivid red in bright, cool conditions, deepening into the 'Ruby Blush' color that gives the popular selection its name, while shaded plants stay mostly green. Water carefully at the soil line rather than from overhead, since the hairy leaf surface holds moisture and can scorch or spot if droplets sit in direct sun. It branches on short stems as it matures, tending toward a low shrublet rather than a single tight rosette, and produces clusters of orange-red, bell-shaped flowers in winter that are a valuable nectar source for hummingbirds where grown outdoors.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a hybrid cultivar it does not come true from seed, so all propagation is vegetative, from either dropped leaves or the freely produced basal offsets.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. 'Fred Ives' is an intergeneric hybrid between Graptopetalum and Echeveria that produces large, open rosettes up to 8 inches across of thick, pointed, powdery leaves in a soft taupe-pink to lavender-grey base color. Strong sun and cool nights push the leaf color toward a coppery pink-orange along the tips, while shaded plants stay a cooler grey-green, so bright, unfiltered light gives the best display. It offsets readily from the base to form a spreading clump and also grows individual leaves into new plants when they detach cleanly, making it one of the easier large-rosette succulents to multiply. Trim the occasional lengthening stem to keep rosettes compact, and repot every couple of years into fresh gritty mix as older plants can become top-heavy for their pot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Lay individual leaves or short stem cuttings on the surface of dry, very well-drained succulent mix in spring; moonstones roots and produces new plantlets readily from detached leaves, which is the standard home propagation method.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, and water only after the soil has dried out completely. Pachyphytum oviferum (moonstones) produces plump, egg-shaped leaves in soft pastel shades of lavender, blue-grey, and pale pink, coated in a powdery white farina that gives the plant its frosted, gumdrop-like look; avoid touching the leaves, since fingerprints permanently remove the protective bloom. The trailing, sprawling stems eventually flop over the edge of a container as they lengthen, so it works well in a shallow pot or hanging arrangement, and old stems can be cut back and re-rooted to renew a tidy rosette shape. Intense, direct afternoon sun in hot climates can scorch the leaves, so bright morning sun with some midday protection gives the best color without burning. In winter, arching stems of coral-red, bell-shaped flowers rise above the foliage on well-grown plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in fall or spring in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; like other aeoniums, pinwheel aeonium is a winter-growing, summer-dormant Canary Islands succulent, so cuttings establish best during the cool season rather than in summer heat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun to part shade, watering moderately from fall through spring and withholding water in summer when growth pauses. Aeonium haworthii (pinwheel aeonium) is smaller and more freely branching than the larger tree aeonium, forming a rounded, multi-stemmed shrublet topped with neat 4-to-5-inch rosettes of blue-green, spoon-shaped leaves edged in a fine red-pink line that gives the compact rosette its 'pinwheel' look. It shares the unusual reverse growing season of its genus, actively growing through cool, moist winters and going semi-dormant with reduced leaf turgor in hot, dry summers, when watering should be cut back sharply. This species is the parent of several popular variegated and colored cultivars, including 'Kiwi' and 'Tricolor', and readily branches from cut stems, making it easy to shape or propagate from tip cuttings. It suits rock gardens, mixed succulent containers, and coastal Mediterranean-style plantings in zone 9-11.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot small nursery plants or separate mature clumps in spring into a very lean, mineral, extremely fast-draining mix with minimal organic matter; living stones need almost no water while establishing and are far more likely to be killed by overwatering than underwatering.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot of very lean, gritty, mineral succulent mix in bright, direct sun, following a strict seasonal watering rhythm rather than a fixed schedule. Lithops (living stones, pebble plants) are southern African mesembs that mimic the pebbles and stones of their native habitat as camouflage from grazing animals, each plant consisting of a single pair of fused, fleshy leaves with a translucent 'window' at the top that admits light to the photosynthetic tissue below while the plant sits nearly buried in the substrate. Each year a new leaf pair emerges from the center and slowly absorbs the old pair, which shrivels and splits away, a process that requires almost no supplemental water; water sparingly in fall as the growing season begins, taper off through winter, and withhold water almost entirely while the old leaves are being reabsorbed in spring, resuming light watering only once new leaves are fully formed. Bright, direct sun year-round is essential to keep the body compact and prevent the plant from stretching; daisy-like white or yellow flowers, larger than the plant body itself, open from the cleft between the leaves in autumn.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Divide offset clumps or root stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; tiger jaws clumps steadily with age, so mature plants are easy to split into several new pots.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering only after the soil has dried out and cutting back further in winter. Faucaria tigrina (tiger jaws) is a South African mesemb related to Lithops, forming pairs of thick, triangular, blue-green leaves edged with soft, white, tooth-like projections that interlock across the opposing leaf pairs like an open jaw, giving the plant its common name; the 'teeth' are soft and harmless rather than sharp spines. Individual rosette pairs are short-lived but the plant continuously produces new pairs from the center, gradually building into a low, spreading clump of interlocking 'jaws' over a few years. Large, daisy-like, bright yellow flowers open in the afternoon sun in autumn, closing again by evening, and are a reliable bloomer even on young plants given enough direct light. Keep the winter rest period dry, since like most South African mesembs it is far more prone to rot from overwatering in cool weather than from drought.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
